bridges.description: Establish that Jesus fulfilled at least part of the Old Testament's predictions.
Connect the Old Testament's covenant, sacrifice, redemption, and messianic themes into a cumulative trajectory toward Jesus.
Show that particular texts and motifs, read in their historical and literary context, correspond to features attributed to Jesus.
Support reasonable confidence that the relevant events in Jesus's life occurred and can serve as fulfillment evidence.
Show that the claim that Jesus fulfilled prophecy has not been demonstrated to a reasonable evidential standard.
Require a prophecy to be identifiable prospectively, specific, and sufficiently unambiguous before a claimed fulfillment.
Require evidence that the reported event actually occurred and fulfilled the prediction rather than merely appearing in a later story.
Challenge Christian readings as retrospective pattern matching where alternative Jewish or ordinary readings remain available.

sections.title: Covenant narrative and messianic identity
sections.rationale: The pro case frames the entire Old Testament as a covenant-redemption trajectory centered on Jesus, while the con case disputes that framework and contrasts it with Jewish expectations.

sections.title: Specificity, interpretation, and prospective prediction
sections.rationale: The central methodological dispute concerns what qualifies as prophecy, how much interpretation is permissible, and whether a prediction must be identifiable before the alleged fulfillment.

sections.title: Historical evidence and verification
sections.rationale: Fulfillment depends on whether relevant claims about Jesus can be held with reasonable confidence and whether story-to-story correspondence supplies independent evidence.

sections.title: Isaiah, Genesis, and typological correspondences
sections.rationale: The speakers directly test the competing methods against Isaiah 53, Genesis 3, Genesis 22, sacrifice motifs, and the reported magic-trick comparison.

selectionBalanceAudit.rationale: Historical evidence contains four distinct con moves: the initial fact-verification burden, the certainty/reasonableness correction, the testimony-and-testing challenge, and the two-part prediction/event requirement. They are independently assessable and cannot be merged without losing the con burden structure. The pro has two load-bearing historical replies: its source-based verification claim and its two-stage method. Other pro material belongs to the covenant, interpretation, or textual-example sections rather than being reclassified to force symmetry.

sections.rationale: The fourth pro row separately preserves the Jewish-convert counterexample; it is distinct from the qualified thesis, the Genesis-to-Exodus trajectory, and the Messiah-role reply.
